name: Portkey AI Gateway
license: MIT (open-source gateway core; the hosted control plane is commercial)
supported_backends: none (gateway layer - forwards to any OpenAI-compatible or native provider endpoint)
supported_formats: passthrough (OpenAI-compatible plus native provider shapes; format-agnostic because it never loads weights)
notable_features: The purest statement of what a gateway layer decides: a weighted distribution over targets that may be different VENDORS or different MODELS, configured as {"strategy":{"mode":"loadbalance"},"targets":[{"provider":"@openai-prod","weight":0.7},...]}. Weights are normalized to sum to 100%, so 5, 3, 1 become 55/33/11%. Default weight 1, minimum 0 - and weight 0 is notable because it 'stops traffic without removing from config', making a provider a config-only kill switch.

Five documented routing patterns covering most fleet topologies: between providers (model comes from the request), between models, multiple API keys for the same provider to spread across per-account rate limits, cost optimization (mostly to a cheap model, a slice to a premium one), and gradual migration (a small percentage to a new model before full rollout).

Sticky load balancing: {"sticky":{"enabled":true,"hash_fields":["metadata.user_id"],"ttl":3600}} with default TTL 3600 s. Mechanism is hash the listed fields, look up the previous target from cache, and reuse it - the gateway-level analogue of a router's session affinity, carrying the same hazard: a bad first assignment persists for the whole TTL.

Sticky sessions use a two-tier cache (in-memory plus Redis) specifically so assignments survive across gateway instances in distributed deployments - an explicit acknowledgement that gateway routing state is shared, not local.
'@provider-slug/model-name' routes automatically, and configs can be created and used from within requests.
The vendor's own cautions are worth keeping: 'Each LLM has different latency and pricing', and weight distribution directly affects spend, so a routing change is a cost change.
hardware_caveats: No local compute: never loads weights, never touches an accelerator. supported_backends is an explicit 'none'.

Weighted routing is not latency-aware. The docs say so - weights are relative shares of traffic and nothing more - so a weight split tuned for cost will send traffic to a slow target at the same rate.

Sticky routing depends on a reachable cache; a cache outage degrades to weighted-random behaviour unless misses are handled, and a two-tier cache means the tiers can disagree about a session's target.

The documented sticky TTL is 3600 s, long relative to a provider's rate limits and longer than most autoscaler reactions - a session pinned to a target that is later drained stays pinned for up to an hour.

Vendor-published gateway latency comparisons are contested in this repo's sources: a competitor's benchmark shows 'large latency advantages over Portkey and LiteLLM' using mock backends under default gateway configurations, which is not the production configuration.
No published throughput ceiling in the sources gathered here, so unlike LiteLLM's documented ~300 RPS bottleneck there is no measured headroom figure to plan against - treat capacity as unmeasured.
best_for: Multi-provider fleets where the routing decision is commercial rather than technical - cost split, canary rollout, or spreading across per-account provider rate limits
Teams wanting one endpoint and one config surface across many vendors, including their own self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers
Gradual model migration, where a weighted percentage with stickiness is the whole feature
Portkey-specific integrations (guardrails, hosted Model Catalog, config-in-request workflow) where ecosystem matters more than the routing core
avoid_for: Single-vendor or single-model deployments, where weighted routing is overhead
Kubernetes-native cache-aware or load-aware pod selection - use an inference gateway with an Endpoint Picker for that, and Portkey above it for policy
Deployments needing per-token quota or GPU-level awareness
Cases where routing state must be authoritative - the sticky cache is a convenience layer, not a source of truth
notes: Recorded as an engine on the same precedent as litellm: a gateway is an engine record because it occupies a layer with no other home in data/. Its distinguishing contribution to the topology layer is that it expresses routing as an explicit WEIGHTED COMMERCIAL POLICY across heterogeneous targets, where the Kubernetes-native gateways express it as a load- or cache-aware pick among replicas of one model. Those are genuinely different jobs and they compose - but stacking both without deciding which owns the placement decision is the failure mode. Note the sticky-routing TTL hazard is structurally the same as the router latching bug recorded separately in this repo (dep-prefixaware-subthreshold-latches-a-bad-first-pick): a routing decision made once and cached for a long lifetime is not re-evaluated when the fleet changes underneath it. Accuracy caveat: routing semantics are quoted from Portkey's own documentation, which is authoritative for its behaviour; the performance characterizations come from a competitor's benchmark page and are recorded only as a caution about methodology, not as measurements.
